Oscar Release

By: Este de Klerk | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
What does June and Barry Steenkamp want to say to Oscar Pistorius, now that he is set to be released from prison? What will the State argue in their appeal case against Judge Masipa's verdict?

Summary:
What does June and Barry Steenkamp want to say to Oscar Pistorius, now that he is set to be released from prison? What will the State argue in their appeal case against Judge Masipa's verdict and where will Oscar Pistorius be serving the remainder of his sentence under house arrest?

Further information:
With only days left before Oscar Pistorius is set to be released from the Kgosi Mampuru II prison in Pretoria after serving ten months of his five-year sentence, the Minister of Justice and Correctional Service, Michael Masutha, is now seeking legal advice on whether the parole board of the Kgosi Mampuru II prison was right to decide to release him under correctional supervision after serving one sixth of his sentence.

Masutha said he was seeking advice on whether the Parole Board's decision was "correct in law and regular" and if it wasn't, whether there was anything that empowered him in law to have the matter revisited.

The Parole Board of the Kgosi Mampuru II prison in Pretoria sat on the 5th of June and made the decision. June and Barry Steenkamp, decided, despite a request from the Parole Board, that they would not want to participate in the process in person, but wrote a letter to the Parole Board, saying that although they had forgiven Oscar Pistorius, serving ten months in prion was not enough for taking a life and it would send out the wrong message.

Minister Masutha is now seeking legal advice after the Progressive Women's Movement of SA opposed Pistorius's release and wrote to him last Thursday on behalf of the 80 political and non-political organisations they represent. It seemed as if PWMSA questioned Pistorius's release during August, which is of course women's month in South Africa. But his release date, the 21st of August, would be exactly ten months after he was sentenced on the 21st of October last year.

Despite releasing a press statement on late Monday, saying they wouldn't grant any media interviews during this week - which also marks what would have been Reeva Steenkamp's 32st birthday - June Steenkamp changed her mind. She is granting us an exclusive interview this week - "in celebration of Reeva's life".

In an article You Magazine carried this week, June and Barry apparently said they had a message for Oscar Pistorius after he would be released. They told the Magazine they wanted to see him and talk to him, but didn't divulge what they wanted to say to him. We will aim to find this out. June also said that she now has to focus on establishing the Reeva Rebecca Steenkamp Trust in aid of abused women and children - that would be Reeva's legacy to the world.

Also on Monday this week, the Director of Public Prosecutions filed its heads of argument as well as a record of the Oscar Pistorius trial at the Supreme Court of Appeal in Bloemfontein.

The papers were filed in preparation of the State’s appeal against the paralympian’s culpable homicide conviction that is due to be heard in November. The state is asking that Pistorius’s conviction be set aside and that he be found guilty of the more serious charge of murder, which could see his sentence upgraded to a minimum of 15 years in prison.

Pistorius is currently serving a five-year prison sentence for killing his girlfriend Reeva Steenkamp on Valentine’s Day in 2013.

The High Court in Pretoria had reserved the following questions of law for the consideration of the Supreme Court of Appeal:

* Whether the principles of dolus eventualis were correctly applied to the accepted facts and the conduct of the accused;

* Whether the Court correctly conceived and applied the legal principles pertaining to circumstantial evidence and/or pertaining to multiple defences by an accused; and

* Whether the Court was correct in its construction and reliance on an alternative version of the accused and that this alternative version was reasonably possibly true.

In its heads of argument, the State claims that the trial court incorrectly applied the principles of dolus eventualis. At the heart of the matter is the question whether Pistorius could foresee that Steenkamp would be killed, but continued shooting, regardless.

“Should it be found that the Court incorrectly applied the principles of dolus eventualis, then a conclusion that the respondent [Pistorius] should have been convicted of murder is, with respect, inescapable”, the State claims in its submission.

“We argue that the only conceivable finding based on the (abovementioned) facts could at a minimum be that, in arming himself, walking to the bathroom with the intention to shoot, whilst knowing that there is a person behind a closed door of a small cubicle and intentionally firing four shots, should be that he intended to kill the person in the cubicle.”

The State goes on to argue that, if the court applied the legal principles pertaining to multiple defences by an accused wrongly, then a finding that the accused’s version was reasonably possibly true would be impossible.

“It is respectfully submitted that an accused’s version must be regarded as ‘inherently improbably’ if ‘he [or she] presents conflicting versions to the court’, so much so that it cannot be reasonably possibly true.”

As for the question of dealing with circumstantial evidence, the State further argues that “not only did the Court a quo exclude relevant evidence, but exhibited a fragmented approach in evaluating the circumstantial evidence.”

Judge Thokozile Masipa had found Pistorius guilty of culpable homicide, not murder, on September 12, 2014. Pistorius had claimed he fired four shots through the locked door of a toilet in his Pretoria home, under the mistaken impression that an intruder was hiding inside. He was also sentenced to three years imprisonment for discharging a firearm in a restaurant. This sentence was suspended for five years, which meant it would only kick in should Pistorius be found guilty of the same or a similar offence within the next five years.

Masipa granted the State leave to appeal last year based on her interpretation of the law, not the facts of the matter.

Press Release:


Oscar Released
Under the cover of darkness, Oscar Pistorius was quietly released from Kgosi Mampuru II Prison in Pretoria, successfully eluding the world's media camped outside. As Oscar prepares to see out the remainder of his five-year sentence under correctional supervision, Carte Blanche asks why his planned release in August was delayed, and what will be argued in the Appeal Court just two weeks from now. And for the first time, Reeva’s father Barry Steenkamp speaks about the ordeal that followed his daughter’s shocking death.


Script:


OSCAR RELEASE SCRIPT

PRODUCER: ESTé DE KLERK

BARRY STEENKAMP: It would be wrong of me to say I feel sorry for him, how could I feel sorry for him? I just thought to myself, man you just brought this onto yourself and you’ve been very lucky with the sentence that has been put onto you, that’s what I thought.

For Reeva Steenkamp’s father, Barry, Oscar Pistorius’s life and future are irrelevant. When Oscar would finally be released from prison for the killing of his beloved daughter, was not something Barry constantly contemplated.

Staying busy, rather, since that fateful day, has been his saving grace - then, Barry says, time seems to go a lot quicker.

BARRY STEENKAMP: I just wish to God it would all come to an end now so that we can all carry on with our lives yes.

It’s in the stillness at the stables where he trains his race horses that he finds solace. Talking about Reeva’s death doesn’t come easy and this is the first South African television interview he has granted since. Reeva was very much a Daddy’s girl, he says.

BARRY STEENKAMP: do you know how often I would ask Reeva to come back to P.E, often, I didn’t want her to be there, but anyway all these things have happened most probably for the good in the end, you will see how people have bucked up, i'm not knocking the justice system but how everybody has woken up to small things that people didn’t take note of before and it has only helped in that way yes.

Barry says that he had been consumed with guilt because he couldn’t protect Reeva on that fateful night.

BARRY STEENKAMP: We have had slight catastrophes in the past with Reeva, with her being ill, with tonsillitis where she had hemorrhaged and everything like that, the day she fell of the horse I was there, I was there on two occasions - but guilty yes, that I wasn’t there the third time.

The world’s media waited in anticipation for Oscar’s release on Tuesday from the Kgosi Mampuru II prison in Pretoria under correctional supervision. In stark contrast, it made little difference to the lives of the Steenkamps, says Reeva’s mother June, who now focuses on building a foundation in Reeva’s name.

JUNE STEENKAMP: She is never coming back, she is gone. I’m happy to take the batten from her and run with it.

Monday morning in the upmarket suburb of Waterkloof ...all was quiet at Oscar’s uncle Arnold’s home. But this changed overnight.
The media that were waiting to catch a glimpse of his release from prison, had all been thwarted. He was released in secrecy already at seven-thirty on Monday night.

DEVI LINK: Oscar will serve the remainder of his five year sentence under correctional supervision here in Waterkloof, surrounded by embassies and tight security.

Tuesday outside Arnold’s house mirrored images of the outside of court a year ago when Oscar was sentenced.
Uncle Arnold was seen leaving early in the morning. The only family statement was made by spokesperson, Annelieze Burgess, who didn’t want to comment on how Oscar was doing.

ANNELIESE BURGESS: Oscar is at home with the family and he will strictly adhere to the conditions.

JUNE STEENKAMP: its not all about him coming out and I know that he would be celebrating coming out, but at the same time they have to remember that she died

The Department of Correctional Service’s spokesperson, Manelisi Wolela, didn’t want to comment on the specific conditions of Oscar’s correctional supervision.

MANELISI WOLELA: It may range from house arrest, it can include regular visits by our community corrections officials, the prohibitions in terms of getting out of the house within a particular period in a day, and the only thing that I can mention which is specific here is what the parole review board instructed. it restricts having and using a fireararm and the second one instructed that there should be continuation of what they call psychotherapy.

This additional recommendation was made by the Parole Review Board, because it felt the psychological therapy Oscar received in prison might not have been sufficient, says Professor Annette van der Merwe, Criminal Procedure Law lecturer at the University of Pretoria.

PROF. ANNETTE VAN DER MERWE: It was his previous psychologist who was involved, but she was an educational psychologist, but they said it should be a clinical psychologist, they want more in-depth therapy for him

DEVI LINK: Oscar was supposed to have been released on the 22nd of August after serving ten months of his five year sentence. But in a surprise move, Minister of Correctional Services, Michael Masutha, blocked his release based on a technicality in the law.

Minister Masutha referred the matter to the Parole Review Board.

Oscar has been sentenced in terms of section 276 (1)(i) of the Criminal Procedure Act – which means that if sentenced for five years imprisonment or less, a prisoner has to serve one sixth of his sentence behind bars. For Oscar that was a period of ten month – ending on the 22nd of August.

But the Department of Correctional Services erred in how his sentence was administered.

PROF. ANNETTE VAN DER MERWE: Section 73 (7a) of this Correctional SAervices Act reads as follows: a person…must serve at least at least once sixth BFORE being considered for placement, unless the court determines otherwise

This didn’t happen in Oscar’s case. Already in June – two months before the expiry of the ten-month period, the Parole Board convened and decided he would be released on the day the ten months ran out.

DEVI: Do you think Oscar was treated unfairly?

PROF. ANNETTE VAN DER MERWE: I think to a certain extent, because of his profile, he was discriminated against.

But Professor van der Merwe says this is how it has always worked – Parole Boards have never strictly followed this section of the Correctional Services Act.

PROF. ANNETTE VAN DER MERWE: This act came into operation in 2004 and no body scrutinised it. From what I understand is that since this event a whole set of guidelines have been issued in the dept and in future all these cases will now be dealt with according to that guidelines

MANELISI WOLELA: We identified a hundred and nine cases that had, as was the concern of the Minister, has not concluded the one sixth of their sentences under custody.

DEVI LINK: Oscar’s taste of partial freedom may be short-lived. In just nine days, the State will argue in the Supreme Court of Appeal why Oscar should have been found guilty of murder.

The Appeal will be heard in the Supreme Court of Appeal in Bloemfontein on the third of November.

The State bases its Heads of Argument on three main issues.

STATE: COURT 1: The State will argue in the Appeal Court that Judge Masipa didn’t correctly apply the principle of Dolus Evetualis – that when firing four shot through the toilet door, Oscar must have known that he could kill someone.

The state will also argue that Judge Masipa did not take into account crucial circumstantial evidence and ask whether she was correct to rely on one of several versions put forward by Oscar Pistorius - and to believe that that version could be reasonably, possibly true, says defence attorney Tyrone Maseko.

TYRONE MASEKO: If Dolus Eventualis is present, if it is shown that the necessary intention in this case is Dolus Eventualis that does not equate to culpable homicide that is murder so and what the state is saying is that, look even if you take Oscar Pistorious's own testimony his own words the things that he has said if you take hat on its own, that on itself is Dolus Eventualis and thats what the court should have said, thats what Gerrie Nell.

Pistorius’s defence, however, contends that Judge Masipa was correct in her decision - that Oscar did perceive some sort of danger, but that he lacked the intention to act unlawfully.

DEVI LINK: Oscar’s legal team will argue that the State is attempting to reintroduce its case of dolus directus – that Oscar killed with intent.

Barry says he will accept the outcome of the Appeal.

BARRY STEENKAMP: Once that has all come to an end it will give us time you know to settle down with the things that we want to do for his family it will give a lot of us like a closure whether its good or bad.

DEVI LINK: Minister of Correctional Services, Michael Masutha, said that Oscar will be compelled to meet with the Steenkamp family. Through their attorney, the Steenkamps said they would do so, when the time was right and away from the public glare.

And however difficult it may be, both June and Barry now want to meet with him.

JUNE STEENKAMP: I would just want him to realise actually what he has taken away from us, how he has destroyed our lives from taking her away.

BARRY STEENKAMP: I think I will get more of a closure one day if I get the chance to speak to Oscar myself, then I feel I will get more of a closure yes. Most probably I won’t have to say anything, most probably I would just have to look at him, but that is what I would like to do one day, yes.

And even though Barry wishes to move forward, the yearning for his beloved Reeva is ever present.

BARRY STEENKAMP: It’s like June and myself and Reeva and Oscar, but how many people are out there with the same problem or the same situation that we’ve got, and I feel so sorry for these people you know, I really understand it and they can understand us but people who have never experience this, they will never understand this, never.






PROMO’S

PROMO 1: 15”
BARRY STEENKAMP: It would be wrong of me to say I feel sorry for him, how could I feel sorry for him?

An exclusive interview with Barry Steenkamp, in the wake of Oscar Pistorius’s release from prison.

PROMO 2: 15”

Oscar Pistorius was secretly released from prison on Monday night. But it makes no difference to the pain the Steenkamps are still feeling.

BARRY STEENKAMP: people who have never experience this, they will never understand this, never.

PROMO 3: 10”
In the wake of Oscar Pistorius’s release from the Kgosi Mampuru II prison under correctional supervision this week, Reeva Steenkamp’s father, Barry, speaks from the heart.

For Reeva Steenkamp’s father, Barry, Oscar Pistorius’s life and future are irrelevant. When Oscar would finally be released from prison for the killing of his beloved daughter, was not something Barry constantly contemplated. Staying busy, rather, since that fateful day, has been his saving grace - then, Barry says, time seems to go a lot quicker. BARRY STEENKAMP: I just wish to God it would all come to an end now so that we can all carry on with our lives yes. It’s in the stillness at the stables where he trains his race horses that he finds solace. Talking about Reeva’s death doesn’t come easy and this is the first South African television interview he has granted since. Reeva was very much a Daddy’s girl, he says. BARRY STEENKAMP: do you know how often I would ask Reeva to come back to P.E, often, I didn’t want her to be there, but anyway all these things have happened most probably for the good in the end, you will see how people have bucked up, i'm not knocking the justice system but how everybody has woken up to small things that people didn’t take note of before and it has only helped in that way yes. Barry says that he had been consumed with guilt because he couldn’t protect Reeva on that fateful night. BARRY STEENKAMP: We have had slight catastrophes in the past with Reeva, with her being ill, with tonsillitis where she had hemorrhaged and everything like that, the day she fell of the horse I was there, I was there on two occasions - but guilty yes, that I wasn’t there the third time. The world’s media waited in anticipation for Oscar’s release on Tuesday from the Kgosi Mampuru II prison in Pretoria under correctional supervision. In stark contrast, it made little difference to the lives of the Steenkamps, says Reeva’s mother June, who now focuses on building a foundation in Reeva’s name. JUNE STEENKAMP: She is never coming back, she is gone. I’m happy to take the batten from her and run with it. Monday morning in the upmarket suburb of Waterkloof ...all was quiet at Oscar’s uncle Arnold’s home. But this changed overnight. The media that were waiting to catch a glimpse of his release from prison, had all been thwarted. He was released in secrecy already at seven-thirty on Monday night. DEVI LINK: Oscar will serve the remainder of his five year sentence under correctional supervision here in Waterkloof, surrounded by embassies and tight security. Tuesday outside Arnold’s house mirrored images of the outside of court a year ago when Oscar was sentenced. Uncle Arnold was seen leaving early in the morning. The only family statement was made by spokesperson, Annelieze Burgess, who didn’t want to comment on how Oscar was doing. ANNELIESE BURGESS: Oscar is at home with the family and he will strictly adhere to the conditions. JUNE STEENKAMP: its not all about him coming out and I know that he would be celebrating coming out, but at the same time they have to remember that she died The Department of Correctional Service’s spokesperson, Manelisi Wolela, didn’t want to comment on the specific conditions of Oscar’s correctional supervision. MANELISI WOLELA: It may range from house arrest, it can include regular visits by our community corrections officials, the prohibitions in terms of getting out of the house within a particular period in a day, and the only thing that I can mention which is specific here is what the parole review board instructed. it restricts having and using a fireararm and the second one instructed that there should be continuation of what they call psychotherapy. This additional recommendation was made by the Parole Review Board, because it felt the psychological therapy Oscar received in prison might not have been sufficient, says Professor Annette van der Merwe, Criminal Procedure Law lecturer at the University of Pretoria. PROF. ANNETTE VAN DER MERWE: It was his previous psychologist who was involved, but she was an educational psychologist, but they said it should be a clinical psychologist, they want more in-depth therapy for him DEVI LINK: Oscar was supposed to have been released on the 22nd of August after serving ten months of his five year sentence. But in a surprise move, Minister of Correctional Services, Michael Masutha, blocked his release based on a technicality in the law. Minister Masutha referred the matter to the Parole Review Board. Oscar has been sentenced in terms of section 276 (1)(i) of the Criminal Procedure Act – which means that if sentenced for five years imprisonment or less, a prisoner has to serve one sixth of his sentence behind bars. For Oscar that was a period of ten month – ending on the 22nd of August. But the Department of Correctional Services erred in how his sentence was administered. PROF. ANNETTE VAN DER MERWE: Section 73 (7a) of this Correctional SAervices Act reads as follows: a person…must serve at least at least once sixth BFORE being considered for placement, unless the court determines otherwise This didn’t happen in Oscar’s case. Already in June – two months before the expiry of the ten-month period, the Parole Board convened and decided he would be released on the day the ten months ran out. DEVI: Do you think Oscar was treated unfairly? PROF. ANNETTE VAN DER MERWE: I think to a certain extent, because of his profile, he was discriminated against. But Professor van der Merwe says this is how it has always worked – Parole Boards have never strictly followed this section of the Correctional Services Act. PROF. ANNETTE VAN DER MERWE: This act came into operation in 2004 and no body scrutinised it. From what I understand is that since this event a whole set of guidelines have been issued in the dept and in future all these cases will now be dealt with according to that guidelines MANELISI WOLELA: We identified a hundred and nine cases that had, as was the concern of the Minister, has not concluded the one sixth of their sentences under custody. DEVI LINK: Oscar’s taste of partial freedom may be short-lived. In just nine days, the State will argue in the Supreme Court of Appeal why Oscar should have been found guilty of murder. The Appeal will be heard in the Supreme Court of Appeal in Bloemfontein on the third of November. The State bases its Heads of Argument on three main issues. STATE: COURT 1: The State will argue in the Appeal Court that Judge Masipa didn’t correctly apply the principle of Dolus Evetualis – that when firing four shot through the toilet door, Oscar must have known that he could kill someone. The state will also argue that Judge Masipa did not take into account crucial circumstantial evidence and ask whether she was correct to rely on one of several versions put forward by Oscar Pistorius - and to believe that that version could be reasonably, possibly true, says defence attorney Tyrone Maseko. TYRONE MASEKO: If Dolus Eventualis is present, if it is shown that the necessary intention in this case is Dolus Eventualis that does not equate to culpable homicide that is murder so and what the state is saying is that, look even if you take Oscar Pistorious's own testimony his own words the things that he has said if you take hat on its own, that on itself is Dolus Eventualis and thats what the court should have said, thats what Gerrie Nell. Pistorius’s defence, however, contends that Judge Masipa was correct in her decision - that Oscar did perceive some sort of danger, but that he lacked the intention to act unlawfully. DEVI LINK: Oscar’s legal team will argue that the State is attempting to reintroduce its case of dolus directus – that Oscar killed with intent. Barry says he will accept the outcome of the Appeal. BARRY STEENKAMP: Once that has all come to an end it will give us time you know to settle down with the things that we want to do for his family it will give a lot of us like a closure whether its good or bad. DEVI LINK: Minister of Correctional Services, Michael Masutha, said that Oscar will be compelled to meet with the Steenkamp family. Through their attorney, the Steenkamps said they would do so, when the time was right and away from the public glare. And however difficult it may be, both June and Barry now want to meet with him. JUNE STEENKAMP: I would just want him to realise actually what he has taken away from us, how he has destroyed our lives from taking her away. BARRY STEENKAMP: I think I will get more of a closure one day if I get the chance to speak to Oscar myself, then I feel I will get more of a closure yes. Most probably I won’t have to say anything, most probably I would just have to look at him, but that is what I would like to do one day, yes. And even though Barry wishes to move forward, the yearning for his beloved Reeva is ever present. BARRY STEENKAMP: It’s like June and myself and Reeva and Oscar, but how many people are out there with the same problem or the same situation that we’ve got, and I feel so sorry for these people you know, I really understand it and they can understand us but people who have never experience this, they will never understand this, never. PROMO’S PROMO 1: 15” BARRY STEENKAMP: It would be wrong of me to say I feel sorry for him, how could I feel sorry for him? An exclusive interview with Barry Steenkamp, in the wake of Oscar Pistorius’s release from prison. PROMO 2: 15” Oscar Pistorius was secretly released from prison on Monday night. But it makes no difference to the pain the Steenkamps are still feeling. BARRY STEENKAMP: people who have never experience this, they will never understand this, never. PROMO 3: 10” In the wake of Oscar Pistorius’s release from the Kgosi Mampuru II prison under correctional supervision this week, Reeva Steenkamp’s father, Barry, speaks from the heart. metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): What does June and Barry Steenkamp want to say to Oscar Pistorius, now that he is set to be released from prison? What will the State argue in their appeal case against Judge Masipa's verdict?
metadata.Summary: What does June and Barry Steenkamp want to say to Oscar Pistorius, now that he is set to be released from prison? What will the State argue in their appeal case against Judge Masipa's verdict and where will Oscar Pistorius be serving the remainder of his sentence under house arrest?
metadata.Further information: With only days left before Oscar Pistorius is set to be released from the Kgosi Mampuru II prison in Pretoria after serving ten months of his five-year sentence, the Minister of Justice and Correctional Service, Michael Masutha, is now seeking legal advice on whether the parole board of the Kgosi Mampuru II prison was right to decide to release him under correctional supervision after serving one sixth of his sentence. Masutha said he was seeking advice on whether the Parole Board's decision was "correct in law and regular" and if it wasn't, whether there was anything that empowered him in law to have the matter revisited. The Parole Board of the Kgosi Mampuru II prison in Pretoria sat on the 5th of June and made the decision. June and Barry Steenkamp, decided, despite a request from the Parole Board, that they would not want to participate in the process in person, but wrote a letter to the Parole Board, saying that although they had forgiven Oscar Pistorius, serving ten months in prion was not enough for taking a life and it would send out the wrong message. Minister Masutha is now seeking legal advice after the Progressive Women's Movement of SA opposed Pistorius's release and wrote to him last Thursday on behalf of the 80 political and non-political organisations they represent. It seemed as if PWMSA questioned Pistorius's release during August, which is of course women's month in South Africa. But his release date, the 21st of August, would be exactly ten months after he was sentenced on the 21st of October last year. Despite releasing a press statement on late Monday, saying they wouldn't grant any media interviews during this week - which also marks what would have been Reeva Steenkamp's 32st birthday - June Steenkamp changed her mind. She is granting us an exclusive interview this week - "in celebration of Reeva's life". In an article You Magazine carried this week, June and Barry apparently said they had a message for Oscar Pistorius after he would be released. They told the Magazine they wanted to see him and talk to him, but didn't divulge what they wanted to say to him. We will aim to find this out. June also said that she now has to focus on establishing the Reeva Rebecca Steenkamp Trust in aid of abused women and children - that would be Reeva's legacy to the world. Also on Monday this week, the Director of Public Prosecutions filed its heads of argument as well as a record of the Oscar Pistorius trial at the Supreme Court of Appeal in Bloemfontein. The papers were filed in preparation of the State’s appeal against the paralympian’s culpable homicide conviction that is due to be heard in November. The state is asking that Pistorius’s conviction be set aside and that he be found guilty of the more serious charge of murder, which could see his sentence upgraded to a minimum of 15 years in prison. Pistorius is currently serving a five-year prison sentence for killing his girlfriend Reeva Steenkamp on Valentine’s Day in 2013. The High Court in Pretoria had reserved the following questions of law for the consideration of the Supreme Court of Appeal: * Whether the principles of dolus eventualis were correctly applied to the accepted facts and the conduct of the accused; * Whether the Court correctly conceived and applied the legal principles pertaining to circumstantial evidence and/or pertaining to multiple defences by an accused; and * Whether the Court was correct in its construction and reliance on an alternative version of the accused and that this alternative version was reasonably possibly true. In its heads of argument, the State claims that the trial court incorrectly applied the principles of dolus eventualis. At the heart of the matter is the question whether Pistorius could foresee that Steenkamp would be killed, but continued shooting, regardless. “Should it be found that the Court incorrectly applied the principles of dolus eventualis, then a conclusion that the respondent [Pistorius] should have been convicted of murder is, with respect, inescapable”, the State claims in its submission. “We argue that the only conceivable finding based on the (abovementioned) facts could at a minimum be that, in arming himself, walking to the bathroom with the intention to shoot, whilst knowing that there is a person behind a closed door of a small cubicle and intentionally firing four shots, should be that he intended to kill the person in the cubicle.” The State goes on to argue that, if the court applied the legal principles pertaining to multiple defences by an accused wrongly, then a finding that the accused’s version was reasonably possibly true would be impossible. “It is respectfully submitted that an accused’s version must be regarded as ‘inherently improbably’ if ‘he [or she] presents conflicting versions to the court’, so much so that it cannot be reasonably possibly true.” As for the question of dealing with circumstantial evidence, the State further argues that “not only did the Court a quo exclude relevant evidence, but exhibited a fragmented approach in evaluating the circumstantial evidence.” Judge Thokozile Masipa had found Pistorius guilty of culpable homicide, not murder, on September 12, 2014. Pistorius had claimed he fired four shots through the locked door of a toilet in his Pretoria home, under the mistaken impression that an intruder was hiding inside. He was also sentenced to three years imprisonment for discharging a firearm in a restaurant. This sentence was suspended for five years, which meant it would only kick in should Pistorius be found guilty of the same or a similar offence within the next five years. Masipa granted the State leave to appeal last year based on her interpretation of the law, not the facts of the matter.
